Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Mariana was twenty-two years old, a single woman living alone in a small apartment in Houston, working as an accountant at a mid-sized firm. She had come to therapy reluctantly, referred by her primary care doctor after she had missed three consecutive weeks of work and was at risk of losing her job. What had brought her to this point, she explained slowly, staring at the floor, was something that had happened two years ago, when she was still living at home with her mother and her younger brother, Mateo.

Mateo had been seven at the time. He had developed a sudden, severe bacterial infection that had led to sepsis. Mariana remembered the night clearly—the way her mother had screamed, the frantic drive to the emergency room, the hours in the waiting room while Mateo was in the ICU. But what she remembered most vividly, what came back to her in moments she could not control, was the taste. She could taste the stale coffee from the hospital vending machine, bitter and metallic, mixed with the dry, recycled air of the waiting room. That taste would return without warning—while she was eating dinner, while she was brushing her teeth, while she was sitting at her desk at work—and it would bring with it the full weight of that night: the fluorescent lights, the beeping monitors, the feeling of her own heart pounding so hard she thought she might die before Mateo did. She tried to push the memory away before it could fully arrive, but the taste was always there first, and the moment she recognized it, she would find herself unable to speak, unable to put into words what was happening inside her.

Mateo had survived. He was healthy now, a boisterous nine-year-old who barely remembered the hospital. But Mariana had not survived in the same way. She had come to believe that she was fundamentally changed, that the happy, easygoing person she had been before had been replaced by someone who was always miserable, always waiting for the next disaster. She felt isolated from everyone around her, set apart by something she could not explain. Her coworkers at the accounting firm would chat about weekend plans, about television shows, about their children, and Mariana would sit at her desk, silent, certain that they could see something wrong with her, that they could sense she was broken.

The silence itself had become a threat. In the open-plan office, when the hum of conversation would suddenly drop—when everyone focused on their spreadsheets at once—Mariana would feel her chest tighten, her breath grow shallow. She had come to believe that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen. She also found herself watching the clock obsessively. If a report took longer than expected to load on her computer, if a colleague was late to a meeting, if her lunch order took more than fifteen minutes, she would assume something bad was happening. Her body would react before her mind could catch up: her heart would race, her palms would sweat, and she would feel a wave of nausea that had no apparent cause. She had learned to excuse herself to the bathroom, to stand in a stall with her eyes closed until the feeling passed, but the cost was accumulating. She had missed deadlines. She had stopped eating lunch with her team. She had begun calling in sick on days when she could not face the silence of the office.

What frightened Mariana most was the helplessness. She had always believed that she could keep her family safe, that if she was careful enough, watchful enough, she could prevent bad things from happening. But Mateo’s illness had taught her otherwise. Now she was certain that she could not stop bad things from happening to her, to anyone she loved. She had stopped visiting her mother’s house because the silence there—the quiet after her mother went to bed, the absence of Mateo’s laughter—felt like a sign that something terrible was imminent. She had stopped answering phone calls from her family, afraid that the news would be bad. She had begun to live inside a small, shrinking world, where the only thing she could control was her own isolation.

She came to therapy because she had finally realized she could not keep her job this way, and without her job, she would have nothing left. She was afraid of what would happen if she let herself remember the hospital fully, afraid that if she stopped monitoring every silence, every delay, something terrible would slip through. But she was also, beneath that fear, hoping that someone could help her find a way back to the person she used to be.
